fixes.explanation: Yes, friend, that's the word. The verse says, "Moab is put to shame, for it has been shattered." Shattered, like the jars in verse 12. The picture holds together (Jeremiah 48:20, 48:12).

That's the plan in Heshbon. The people there say, "Come, let us cut her off from nationhood." It's a plot to wipe Moab off the map as a nation. I think that's a heavy plan to read about (Jeremiah 48:2).
No songs on this road, friend. The text says they weep bitterly as they go up to Luhith. The mood there is tears, not war songs (Jeremiah 48:5).
Silence isn't what the verse describes, baker. The text says they weep bitterly as they go. Weeping is what fills that ascent (Jeremiah 48:5).
That's right. The cry on the way down to Horonaim says, "Flee! Run for your lives!" It's a cry to run, and run now. Not a cry to stroll (Jeremiah 48:5-6).

Yes, baker. Chemosh goes into exile with his priests and officials. Chemosh is the god of the Moabites (1 Kings 11:33), and here he's the one going into exile. That's exactly what the verse says (Jeremiah 48:7).
No safekeeping in this verse, baker. The text says Chemosh will go into exile with his priests and officials. They're the ones leaving, not staying to keep anything safe (Jeremiah 48:7).
Not quite, friend. The LORD says the destroyer will move against every city, and "…not one town will escape." Every city is on the list, so there are no exceptions (Jeremiah 48:8).

Yes, baker. The text says, "…his flavor has remained the same, and his aroma is unchanged." Wine that never gets poured from vessel to vessel just sits there, settled on its dregs. The verse says Moab has not gone into exile (Jeremiah 48:11).
Sour isn't in the verse, friend. The LORD says, "…his flavor has remained the same, and his aroma is unchanged." The point is that it hasn't changed (Jeremiah 48:11).

That's not what these wanderers are said to do, baker. The text says they will pour him out, empty his vessels and shatter his jars. Pouring and shattering are the actions the verse names (Jeremiah 48:12).
Yes, baker. The LORD says, "Then Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh…" Chemosh is the god of the Moabites (1 Kings 11:33). Back in verse 7, he's the one going into exile (Jeremiah 48:13, 48:7).
Baal isn't the name in this verse, friend. The LORD says, "Then Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh…" Chemosh is the god of the Moabites (1 Kings 11:33; Jeremiah 48:13).

I get why you'd think so, friend, but the text says the opposite. The King says the best of Moab's young men "…have gone down in the slaughter…" They don't win in this verse. They fall (Jeremiah 48:15).
That's a lot of waiting, friend. But the verse says, "Moab’s calamity is at hand, and his affliction is rushing swiftly." It's close, not far off, so generations don't fit this one (Jeremiah 48:16).

Spared would be good news, baker, but the text doesn't say it. The verse says, "Moab is put to shame, for it has been shattered." Back in verse 8, the LORD says not one town will escape (Jeremiah 48:20, 48:8).
